Slovenia Grapples with Rapid Currency Depreciation as Economic Crisis Deepens

Slovenia is facing mounting economic turmoil as the national currency, the euro-linked tolar, has plunged sharply against the euro in recent weeks, sending shockwaves through the country’s financial system and disrupting business activity across multiple sectors.

The depreciation, which began in late April, accelerated this week, with the tolar falling by 18% against the euro since Monday, according to figures released by the National Bank of Slovenia. The central bank has intervened twice in the foreign exchange markets over the past ten days, but with limited effect.

“Market confidence has been severely shaken by ongoing fiscal uncertainty and concerns over public debt sustainability,” said Dr. Alenka Pokorn, chief economist at the Ljubljana Institute for Economic Studies. “The sharp fall of the tolar is feeding inflationary pressures and making imports more expensive, creating a vicious cycle.”

The immediate impacts of the currency slide are being felt most acutely by import-dependent sectors. Petromix, a leading fuel distributor, warned that wholesale fuel prices will rise by at least 12% next week. Meanwhile, construction firms such as Gradbenik d.o.o. report that the cost of imported materials has soared, forcing them to renegotiate contracts or suspend work on several projects.

Retailers are also feeling the strain. The Slovenian Retailers Association said in a statement, “Our members are seeing daily price changes from suppliers and are struggling to maintain stable pricing for consumers.” The association estimates that food prices have increased by an average of 7% in the past month alone.

Unions have called for urgent government action to protect real wages and jobs. “Workers cannot bear the brunt of this crisis,” said Jure Novak, spokesperson for the Confederation of Slovenian Trade Unions. “We demand targeted subsidies for essential goods and an immediate review of wage agreements in the most affected sectors.”

Finance Minister Mateja Hribar addressed parliament on Thursday, announcing the formation of a crisis task force and pledging to “restore market confidence and prevent further destabilization.” The ministry is reportedly considering temporary capital controls and import tariffs, though no concrete measures have been unveiled.

International observers are closely monitoring the situation. The European Central Bank has offered technical assistance, but has not signaled any direct intervention.

With the tolar’s value continuing to wobble and inflation climbing, many Slovenian businesses are bracing for a protracted period of instability. “We are preparing for the worst but hoping for a swift policy response,” said Andrej Zupan, CEO of logistic provider SloTrans. “The next few weeks will be critical for Slovenia’s economic future.”
